questions.title: Why is a statutory right to an investigation insufficient for Article III standing under Summers?
questions.question_body: I'm reading *America First Legal Foundation v. Greer* and the court cites *Summers v. Earth Island Inst.* to say a 'procedural right in vacuo' isn't enough for standing. AFL argued OSC violated its procedural right to an investigation under 5 U.S.C. § 1216. I thought if a statute says an agency 'shall' investigate, that creates a legally protected interest. Why does the court require an additional 'concrete interest' beyond the procedural right itself, and what qualifies as that concrete interest in this context?

questions.title: How does the 'independent actor' doctrine affect causation in standing analysis here?
questions.question_body: In the standing analysis, the court rejects AFL's argument that OSC's failure to investigate caused the denial of FOIA records. The court lists a chain: OSC investigates -> MSPB sanctions -> DOJ produces records. I'm confused about why this chain is 'too speculative.' If OSC is mandated to investigate, isn't it reasonable to assume they would find a violation and the MSPB would act? How does the 'independent actor' doctrine (citing *FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine*) specifically break the causal link between OSC's inaction and the injury?

questions.title: Does 5 U.S.C. § 1216 create an entitlement to information for informational standing purposes?
questions.question_body: The court discusses 'informational standing' and says AFL lacks an entitlement to receive information under § 1216. AFL argued that if OSC investigates, they might provide notices required under § 1214. The court says § 1214 notice requirements are discretionary in § 1216 investigations. I'm struggling with the statutory interpretation here: § 1216(c) says OSC acts 'in the same way as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved.' Doesn't that language import the mandatory notice provisions of § 1214, or is there a distinction between the *investigation* method and the *notice* obligations?

questions.title: How does Heckler v. Chaney influence the redressability prong of standing in this case?
questions.question_body: The court mentions *Heckler v. Chaney* regarding agency enforcement discretion when discussing redressability. AFL wants the court to order OSC to investigate. Even if the court orders an investigation, OSC might still decide not to take disciplinary action. How does the presumption against judicial review of non-enforcement decisions affect the 'likely to be redressed' requirement? Does it mean a plaintiff can never get standing to compel an investigation unless the outcome is guaranteed?

questions.title: Why did the D.C. Circuit vacate and remand for jurisdictional dismissal instead of affirming the merits dismissal?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed AFL's case for 'failure to state a claim' (a merits-based dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)). However, the D.C. Circuit concluded AFL lacks Article III standing (a jurisdictional issue). The opinion states they 'vacate the district court's judgment and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.' Why is this procedural distinction important? Why can't the appellate court just affirm the dismissal on alternative grounds?

questions.title: Why did the court decline to resolve the conflict between 5 U.S.C. § 1216 and § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)?
questions.question_body: The district court ruled that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC's power under § 1216, but the D.C. Circuit says 'we need not decide' this issue because of the standing failure. I'm confused about the relationship between these two statutes. If the court determined there was no standing, does it mean the statutory conflict is irrelevant, or is this an example of the constitutional avoidance canon? Shouldn't the court clarify the statutory scheme for future cases even if this plaintiff lacks standing?
